title: The Journeys of Paul, c. 46–60 CE
summary: Follow the apostle Paul across the Roman Mediterranean, from Antioch to Cyprus, Galatia, Greece and finally Rome, and see how roads, sea lanes and cities helped early Christianity spread.

sides.name: Roman Empire
sides.description: The Roman Empire under Claudius (41–54) and Nero (54–68)

moves.name: Paul and Barnabas: Antioch to the coast
Paul and Barnabas: home to Antioch
Paul to the Council of Jerusalem
Paul the prisoner: Malta to Puteoli
Paul the prisoner: the Appian Way

events.title: Sent out from Antioch
events.text: The church at Antioch, where followers of Jesus were first called 'Christians', sends out Barnabas and Paul (Acts 13).

events.title: Paphos: the proconsul
events.text: The Roman governor of Cyprus, Sergius Paulus, hears Paul's message (Acts 13:6–12).

events.title: Stoned at Lystra
events.text: Opponents stone Paul and leave him for dead, but he recovers and goes on to Derbe (Acts 14:19–20).

events.title: Council of Jerusalem
events.text: Church leaders decide that non-Jewish believers do not have to follow the whole Law of Moses, including circumcision (Acts 15).

events.title: The 'Macedonian call'
events.text: Paul has a vision of a man saying 'Come over to Macedonia and help us' and crosses into Europe (Acts 16:9).

events.title: Lydia; jailed at Philippi
events.text: Lydia, a trader in purple cloth, becomes the first known believer in Europe. Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed (Acts 16).

events.title: Speech at the Areopagus
events.text: Paul debates philosophers in Athens and speaks of an altar 'to an unknown god' (Acts 17).

events.title: 18 months in Corinth
events.text: Paul works as a tentmaker with Priscilla and Aquila. He writes his letters to the Thessalonians, among the oldest writings in the New Testament.

events.title: Riot at Ephesus
events.text: Silversmiths who make shrines of the goddess Artemis fear for their trade and start a riot in the theatre (Acts 19).

events.title: Letter to the Romans
events.text: From Corinth Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, a city he has not yet visited.

events.title: Arrested in Jerusalem
events.text: A crowd attacks Paul in the Temple. Roman soldiers arrest him, and he is held at Caesarea for two years (Acts 21–26).

events.title: Shipwrecked on Malta
events.text: After two weeks in a storm, the ship runs aground. All 276 people on board reach the shore (Acts 27).

events.title: Arrives in Rome
events.text: Paul lives two years under house arrest, 'welcoming all who came to see him' (Acts 28:30–31).

story.title: A connected world
story.text:
In the first century CE the **Roman Empire** ruled the whole Mediterranean. Roman **roads**, safe **sea lanes**, a shared language (**Greek**) and Jewish communities in many cities made it possible for ideas to travel fast.

**Paul** (Saul) was a Jew from **Tarsus** and a Roman citizen. He had persecuted the first followers of Jesus, then became one of their leaders after an experience on the road to **Damascus**.

question.prompt: Which of these did the most to help a new movement spread across the Mediterranean?
choices: Roman roads, sea routes and a common language
A single religion that everyone already shared
question.explain: The Empire was religiously diverse. What connected it was infrastructure and the Greek language, the same Greek the New Testament was written in.

story.title: The first journey
story.text:
Sent out by the church at **Antioch**, Paul and **Barnabas** sailed to **Cyprus**, then crossed to the mountains of **Galatia** in what is now Turkey. They usually began by speaking in the local **synagogue**, then to non-Jews (**Gentiles**).

They met both welcome and hostility. At **Lystra** Paul was stoned and left for dead. On the way home they visited each new community again to appoint leaders.

story.title: Jews and Gentiles: the Council of Jerusalem
story.text:
As many non-Jews joined, a big question arose: did they have to become Jewish and keep the whole **Law of Moses**? Around 49 CE leaders met in **Jerusalem** and decided they did not.

This decision helped turn a Jewish renewal movement into a faith open to people of every nation.

question.prompt: Why was the Council of Jerusalem so important for the spread of Christianity?
choices: It removed a big barrier for non-Jews who wanted to join
It made Christianity the official religion of Rome
It ended the persecution of Christians
question.explain: Rome did not adopt Christianity until the 300s, and persecution went on for centuries. The council's decision on circumcision and the Law opened the door to Gentiles.

story.title: Into Europe
story.text:
On his second journey, with **Silas** (and later **Timothy**), Paul crossed from **Troas** into **Macedonia**: the first time the message reached Europe. In **Philippi** a businesswoman named **Lydia** believed, and Paul and Silas were beaten and jailed.

In **Athens** Paul debated philosophers. In **Corinth**, a busy port, he stayed **18 months**, working as a tentmaker and writing letters to the believers he had left behind.

question.prompt: Click on the map where Paul first preached in Europe.
question.explain: Philippi, in Macedonia (northern Greece). It was a Roman colony on the Via Egnatia, the great road from the Aegean to the Adriatic.

story.title: Ephesus and the letters
story.text:
Paul spent nearly **three years** in **Ephesus**, one of the largest cities of the Empire. So many people turned away from the goddess **Artemis** that the silversmiths who sold her shrines started a riot.

Paul kept in touch with distant churches by **letters**: to the Corinthians, the Galatians and the Romans. These letters, written in the 50s CE, are some of the earliest Christian writings we have.

story.title: Prisoner, storm and shipwreck
story.text:
In **Jerusalem** Paul was attacked by a crowd and arrested by Roman soldiers. As a **Roman citizen** he appealed to the emperor, so he was sent to Rome under guard.

Sailing late in the season was dangerous. A storm drove the ship west for two weeks until it was wrecked on **Malta**, but all 276 people aboard survived.

question.prompt: Why was Paul sent to Rome instead of being tried in Judea?
choices: As a Roman citizen he had the right to appeal to Caesar
He asked to see the Colosseum
question.explain: Roman citizenship gave legal rights, including appeal to the emperor. Judea did have Roman governors (Felix, then Festus), and the Colosseum was not built until the 70s CE.

story.title: Rome
story.text:
Paul reached **Rome** along the **Appian Way** and lived two years under house arrest, receiving visitors. Christian tradition says he was executed under **Nero** in the 60s CE.

Within 300 years the faith he helped spread had become the largest in the Empire. Historians still debate exactly how and why it grew so fast, but the cities, roads and sea lanes you have followed here were a big part of the answer.

sources: The Acts of the Apostles, chapters 13–28; Paul's letters (Galatians, 1–2 Corinthians, Romans)
F. F. Bruce, Paul: Apostle of the Heart Set Free (1977)
Eckhard J. Schnabel, Paul the Missionary: Realities, Strategies and Methods (2008)
Dates follow the common chronology and are approximate (±1–2 years).
